Judgement
Introduction
This Application has been instituted by the 1st Petitioner, who is a body corporate limited by
guarantee, in dual capacity. On one hand, this Application is filed as a Public Interest Litigation
(PIL), whilst on the other hand, it represents the 2nd Petitioner as the next friend, who physically
cannot come and make an application before this Court, despite the fact that the 2nd Petitioner
is considered as one of the most intelligent animals on Earth; the main differences between a
human and the 2nd Petitioner and its relatives are that humans communicate with its own species
using its own language whilst the 2nd Petitioner cannot understand and communicate using this
human language, except when trained to respond in a specific way to commands received in
the human language, and the 2nd Petitioner does not have hands similar to humans to perform
certain activities.
However, animals are considered property in Sri Lanka; even ownership of an elephant can be
acquired or transferred once a wild elephant is domesticated. However, there is still a question
as to whether an elephant can seek to have rights declared by a court of law, unless such rights
are recognised by the courts depending on the source of law. Although, there is a debate on this
issue, in some jurisdictions, their rights have been recognised, including the right to life, despite
the fact that they cannot appear before a court and make a complaint.1

1 Case “Mona Estrellita” (Rights of Nature and Animals as Subjects of Rights) [253-20-JH/22] Constitutional Court of Ecuador, 27.01.2022); Cuqui Brown [Habeas Corpus 789-22-JH] (Provincial Court of Justice of Napo, Ecuador, 09.08.2022); Narayan Dutt Bhatt v. Union of India 2018 SCC OnLine Utt 645 (Uttarakhand High Court, 4 July 2018); Karnail Singh and Others v. State of Haryana CRR-533-2013 (Punjab and Haryana High Court, 31 May 2019); AFADA v. Metropolitan Corporation Islamabad and Others PLD 2021 Islamabad 6 (High Court of Islamabad, 21 May 2020).
Therefore, 2nd Petitioner is represented by the 1st Petitioner as a next friend.
After issuance of formal notice, this was argued before me on 20.01.2026; hence, this
judgement.
The Petitioners' grievance
The 1st Petitioner is a body corporate incorporated under the Companies Act No. 7 of 2007,
and it is limited by guarantee. The 2nd Petitioner is an elephant X, whose biological name is
identified as “Elephas Maximus Maximus”, and resides in the Gal Oya-Minneriya area, freely
moving around and having access to the protected areas declared under the Fauna and Flora
Protection Ordinance.
The 1st Petitioner inter alia has undertaken to protect the environment and raise environmental
issues in courts and with other authorities, and to protect the environment's fauna and flora for
the present and future generations.
Furthermore, in the course of its activities, it has already undertaken litigation in the nature of
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) before this Court, as well as before the Supreme Court in
Fundamental Rights applications. Thus, the 1st Petitioner dedicates its services to the public to
protect the environment.
As for the Respondents, the 1st Respondent is the Attorney General, who is cited in this
Application as a party representing the Republic of Sri Lanka. The 2nd Respondent is the
Director General of Wildlife Conservation, the 3rd Respondent is the General Manager of
Railways, and the 4th Respondent is the Central Environmental Authority established under the
National Environmental Act No. 47 of 1980.
The immediate issue arising in this Application has arisen due to the accident that took place
by the collision of a certain herd of elephants with a moving train, popularly known for
identification purposes as the “Meenagaya” train, being an express train operated by the
Railway Department, where the 3rd Respondent is the head, which was coming from Batticaloa
bound Colombo.
In this regard, it is alleged by the Petitioners that the 2nd Petitioner, who was also part of the
said herd, met with the said accident which occurred on 25.04.2025 and was severely injured
by the said accident. Six or more elephants of the same herd died on the spot, having succumbed
to injuries sustained in the said accident, while some died later.
Accordingly, the 2nd Petitioner has a personal interest in the litigation, whilst the 1st Petitioner,
representing the people of this country, is moving the Court in the cause of the 2nd Petitioner
and the rest of the wildlife, mainly including elephants.
Furthermore, it is also asserted in the Petition by the Petitioners that the 2nd Respondent is under
a statutory duty to prepare national plans for the purpose of protecting wild animals,
particularly wild elephants, living in the protected areas declared as national reserves or strict
nature reserves, which are meant basically for elephants and other species.
In addition, it is also stated in the Petition that the Northern Railway Line and Eastern Railway
Line pass through protected areas, where on either side of the said lines, there are jungles
roamed by elephants and other species, and particularly, the Eastern Line passes through dense
jungle, famous mainly for elephants inter alia other species of animals.
It is further alleged by the Petitioners that the 2nd Respondent has not taken any action or
implemented any national plan until the accident took place, while the 3rd Respondent also has
failed to take steps or actions to avoid such accidents.
Therefore, it is alleged that a Writ of Mandamus lies against the Respondents, compelling them
to prepare a national plan, if there is none, and to implement the national plan if there is one.
In particular, a writ lies against the 2nd Respondent to take action for the protection of wild
elephants where trains operate on the Northern and Eastern Lines, where elephants and other
species of animals freely roam around in the protected areas through which the said lines lie.
After the issuance of formal notice, no Objections were filed, despite several dates were
obtained for that purpose.
The Petitioners assert that on February 19th, 2025, Wednesday at around 11.30 p.m., the
Colombo-bound "Meenagaya" express train travelling from Batticaloa to Colombo collided
with a herd of elephants, of which the 2nd Petitioner was a member; thereby, the said collision
resulted in six of the elephants dying on the spot, whilst the remaining two elephants were
seriously injured, including the 2nd Petitioner. Later, the other injured elephant also died,
thereby resulting in the deaths of seven elephants all together. Thus, to establish this, the
Petitioner has annexed P2-A, P2-B, and P2-C, including reports and photographs of the
derailed train engine, with the Police and Railway teams investigating the matter.
Furthermore, it is alleged that collisions between elephants and trains frequently happen on the
Northern Railway Line, particularly around Elephant Pass, which is popularly known as the
Northern Line and on the Mannar Line, in addition to that, very often on the Eastern Line. A
summary of the study published is marked as P3.
In addition to that, to establish the same, a news item with relevant photographs which appeared
in the 'Sunday Times' is marked as P4.
Thus, it is alleged that the 2nd Petitioner and its relatives and its species are in real danger, in
addition to the other species of animals who cannot come forward and make complaints in the
Courts of Law, where the law courts are supposedly meant for humans.
It is further alleged that there has been dereliction of performance of the duties by the 2nd to 4th
Respondents, resulting in the said collision. In furtherance, it is asserted that the reconstruction
of the Northern and Eastern Railways, particularly the Northern Railway, including the Mannar
Line, which branches off at Madawachchi from the Northern Line and goes right up to Mannar,
lies through dense jungle areas where the Government has identified and declared elephant
habitats and strict natural reserves as protected areas for elephants and other species to roam
around.
After the war, with the setting up and reconstruction of infrastructure, the railway operation
timetable has been in full operational after 2012; to establish the same, the Petitioners have
filed two documents marked as P6 and P7, respectively, the reports from the printed media that
the Northern and Eastern Lines operate at full operational capacity.
The Petitioners further assert that there are several other national parks and protected areas for
elephants and other species; Kaudulla is one national park established in 2002 by the Gazette
Notification made under the Flora and Fauna Protection Ordinance. Kaudulla is located under
the irrigation plan led by King Mahasen, and from time to time, the Department of Irrigation
is also involved in maintaining it; the Kaudulla Park is located around Minneriya National Park,
Hurulu Eco Park, Gal Oya Eco Park and Wasgamuwa National Park, where elephants are
constantly roaming.
Further, the Eastern Railway Line from Colombo to Batticaloa also passes through the said
dense jungle where elephants roam; copies indicating the active railway network and national
parks situated in close proximity are indicated in the two maps marked as P8 and P9, annexed
to the Petition.
The Petitioners further annex the Extra Ordinary Gazette marked as P10, to establish the
regulations published under the National Environmental Act.
The Petitioners further annexed P11A and P11B, illustrating two study reports on the problems
of accidents which resulted in elephant killings, to establish the gravity of the complaint of the
Petitioners.
To further establish this, the Petitioners have annexed letters written to the relevant authorities,
to establish the complaints made by them, marked as P12 and P13.
In addition to that, the Petitioners have referred to the Fundamental Rights application filed
before the Supreme Court, to establish the rights of the 2nd Petitioner and certain parties.
Relief sought
Therefore, for the dereliction of duties on the part of the Respondents, the Petitioners seek the
intervention of this Court by this Application, seeking inter alia the following relief;
b) Issue a mandate in the nature of a writ of Mandamus directing the 2nd and/or 4th
Respondents to call on the 3rd Respondent to submit an Initial Environmental
Examination and/or Environmental Impact Assessment for the railway lines and
railway operations in the North, East and North Central and Wayamba Provinces in
terms of the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance and the National Environmental
Act and to condition permission for the operation of the said railway lines with
appropriate and meaningful preventive and mitigatory measures with regard, among
others, train-elephant collisions;
c) Issue a mandate in the nature of a writ of Mandamus directing the 2nd Respondents
to prepare a Management Plan for all National Reserves including a plan for protection
of wildlife and avoiding deaths and injuries to animals due to development of public
transport infrastructure in areas within close proximity to National reserves, in
accordance with the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance;
d) Make an Order;
a. Report periodically to this Court on the action taken by the 2nd and/or the 4th
Respondents with regard to the above orders and the subsequent action taken by the
2nd and/or the 4th Respondents;
b. As an interim measure pending the final determination of this application, order the
establishment of a Committee comprising of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th Respondents, a nominee
of the Honourable Attorney General, and other civil society organizations and elephant
experts as to the 1st Respondent shall seem appropriate to formulate an emergency
framework to encompass inter alia, the following;
i. Identification of High-Risk elephant-train collision Railway Stretches and the
development of appropriate mitigation measures, including
"go slow" zones with speed specification;
ii. Take appropriate disciplinary action against railway locomotive and Wildlife
Protection Officers who fail to respect the speed specifications that exist and
are put in place now or in the future, including prosecuting railway locomotive
drivers for "killing" and/or "injuring" elephants under the Fauna and Flora
Protection Ordinance;
iii. Interdepartmental Coordination between the office of the 2nd Respondent
and 3rd Respondent;
iv. Strengthening the role and responsibility of the liaison officers of the 2nd
Respondent on board trains operated under the 3rd Respondent, including
publicly recording and reporting train speeds between identified elephant-train
conflict areas;
v. Sensitization and Training of the officials of the 3rd Respondent to minimize
train collisions with elephants;
vi. Speed Regulations in proximity to Elephant Corridors and National
Reserves;
vii. Adoption of Technology-based and non-technology-based Mitigation and
preventive Measures; and
viii. To file the same in Your Lordship's Court by way of a report and thereafter
to monitor implementation of the mitigatory and preventive measures and their
success and update Your Lordship's Court periodically by way of monitoring
reports;
The Respondents have not filed any Objections. Instead, the Senior State Counsel, Ms.
Kahawita has only filed post-argument Written Submissions for and on behalf of the
Respondents.
In the Written Submissions filed by Ms. Kahawita, she has referred to the fact that there is a
recognised human-elephant conflict which has been there for decades. To minimise the said
conflict, a committee had been appointed in 1957, headed by Mr. K. Somasuntharam as the
Chairperson, and the said Committee also included personalities such as Dr. R.L. Spittel, who
was an environmentalist wildlife enthusiast, wildlife flora and fauna conservationist, and above
all, a prolific writer. In the report filed by the said Committee, the human-elephant conflict has
been identified, and therefore, certain measures have been suggested in the same.
Further, Ms. Kahawita brought to our notice that the same issue has been raised in the Writ
Application bearing No. 420/423/430 & 433/2021, where His Lordship Justice Dr. Sobitha
Rajakaruna (as he then was) had given a judgement.
Action taken by the Respondents
It is also the Respondents' position that the Respondents have identified the main areas where
this human-elephant conflict is seriously affected due to train accidents.
Furthermore, Ms. Kahawita has also referred to the steps taken by various State agencies
pursuant to the meetings held on 15.02.2025 and 18.03.2025 after the collision of the train
resulting in the death of several elephants including causing injury and pain to the 2nd Petitioner.
Therefore, not only the Department of Railway, but even the Wildlife Department has taken
actions with regard to eliminating or at least minimising such accidents; this is also summarised
in the Written Submissions filed for and on behalf of the Respondents.
In addition to that, the Railway Department has also taken various steps, including installing
Luminous signals, clearing railway tracks to allow the train drivers to see the wild elephants
better, identifying places where wild elephants use for crossing the railway lines, effecting
appropriate changes to the train timetable especially to the train travelling at night from the
Colombo Fort to Trincomalee route, and identifying high-risk areas where accidents normally
take place with the elephants, and the brake systems that have been changed in the locomotives
particularly of "Meenagaya", which allows the trains to halt quickly.
Room for action
However, as brought to our notice by the Counsel for the Petitioners, that even in the Written
Submissions of the Respondents, nowhere is it mentioned that train drivers have been properly
educated, and no speed limit has been indicated for between the sections identified as "elephant
corridors" or where the elephants choose as crossings; no action plan has been implemented to
minimise the speed between sections. Therefore, there is still room for further actions to be
taken by the Railway Department.
As such, it is my view as sought by the Petitioners, from time-to-time, reports must be called
for by the Railway Department; therefore, the writs sought by the Petitioners lie in that respect.
On the other hand, the Petitioners have argued, both orally as well as in their written
submissions, as to why they have filed this Application in this Court; although the 2nd to 4th
Respondents would have taken action within the purview of their respective mandates in
protecting the 2nd Petitioner and the species to which it belongs, including other animal species
and flora and fauna, further intervention of this Court has become necessary as accidents
continue to take place.
Before the entire country became a Crown Colony in 1815s, there were no proper roads
anywhere in the country except footpaths. The Kandyan territory was secluded and remained
a natural fortress and remained protected from invasion because of its natural situation. Even
during the Kandyan campaigns to conquer the Kandyan Provinces, which took place in the
1815s, troops marched only on footpaths through three different routes.
However, after the Kandyan Rebellion of 1818, the British Government decided to establish a
proper road network in order to keep the Kandyan areas under control. Thereafter, with the
development of coffee plantations, as well as tea, rubber, and coconut cultivation, a plantation
economy developed under British rule, and, with the increasing need for transport services, the
railway system was introduced.2
However, the Northern and Eastern railway lines were laid during the latter phase of British
rule, particularly in the early 1900s, when railway lines were constructed through thick jungle
areas where there were numerous encounters with wildlife, some of which remain recorded in
folklore and popular literature, including the “Leopard of Punani”. Then, the rulers were not
2 S.V. Balasingham, The Administration of Sir Henry Ward: Governor of Ceylon 1855-1860 (Tisara Prakasakayo 1968).
interested in paying any attention to animal life, in whose benefit certain areas were declared
as protected areas, sanctuaries, or natural reserves; nevertheless, they built the railway lines
through the very same protected areas where the 2nd Petitioner and his relatives and other
species of animals use as their natural habitat.
However, during the War which escalated in 1983 up until 2009, the railroads on the Northern
Line beyond Vavuniya and the Eastern Line did not operate; even the Eastern Line was not in
full operational status. However, with the cessation of hostilities between the warring parties,
there was a resumption of railway operations on those lines officially from 2012, as reflected
in P6 and P7 annexed to the Petition.
However, with the development of the railway and roadway network, human habitation
gradually, not only encroached upon, but also started invading animal habitats, particularly in
the buffer zones of these jungle areas, and from the very beginning the human-elephant conflict
came to the forefront.
However, other animals also faced the same threat of extinction.
Nevertheless, the elephant is a symbolic icon in Sri Lankan culture, and therefore, in the late
1980s, the Government proclaimed the elephant as the 'National animal' due to its historical
and cultural importance, where it remains an iconic and symbolic figure.
I wish to juxtapose to quote from a poem titled, "Elephant", written by the famous English
writer of the novel, "Lady Chatterley's Lover" (1928), D.H. Lawrence, on the ceremonial
elephants who participate in the Esala Perahera of Kandy;3
More elephants, tong, tong-tong, loom up,
3 D.H. Lawrence, Birds, Beasts and Flowers (Martin Secker Limited 1923), 169-175 <https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/60337/pg60337-images.html#ELEPHANT> accessed 08 September 2026.
Huge, more tassels swinging, more dripping fire of new cocoa-nut cressets
High, high flambeaux, smoking of the east;
And scarlet hot embers of torches knocked out of the sockets among bare feet of
elephants and men on the path in the dark.
And devil dancers luminous with sweat, dancing on to the shudder of drums,
Tom-toms, weird music of the devil, voices of men from the jungle singing;
Endless, under the Prince.
The 2nd Petitioner's grievance before this Court epitomizes the threat that the 2nd Petitioner and
his relatives face, not only of death but also of extinction. Therefore, it is our duty to protect
the 2nd Petitioner.
Therefore, the 2nd Respondent, being the Director General of Conservation of Wildlife, should
take action and must inform and report to this Court at regular intervals as to the measures he
has taken to implement the national plan, if any, or prepare one and implement the same in due
course.
Secondly, the 3rd Respondent, being the General Manager of Railways, should also report from
time to time as to the measures he has taken to minimize railway accidents involving animals,
particularly elephants, within the identified zones, especially along the Northern and Eastern
railway lines, where several elephant passes or crossing areas have been identified as depicted
in documents P8 and P9 (the plans).
Action recommended
Therefore, it is my view that the 3rd Respondent, being the General Manager of Railways,
should be directed to report to this Court as to the action the Railway Department has taken at
all levels to train locomotive drivers, whom they refer to as pilots, who are responsible not only
for the safety of the passengers whom they transport daily but also for minimizing
environmental damage caused by reckless driving at excessive speeds without considering the
impact on the environment and animal life. They should not remain oblivious, or purposely
oblivious, to the fact that there are elephant crossings along the railway lines. The same should
be extended to the Railway guards who are responsible for managing the trains.
The General Manager of Railways should take steps to identify the relevant stretches of railway
track where elephant crossings or elephant passes have been identified, and drivers should be
instructed and provided with continuous training, including simulator-based training similar to
that provided to aeroplane pilots, in order to avoid accidents and minimize the impact on flora
and fauna, including that caused by noise pollution.
Further, the drivers and guards must also be trained to regulate speed appropriately within such
identified zones, allowing sufficient time to travel from the point of commencement to the point
of end of those areas while complying with prescribed speed limits. Those who fail to follow
such instructions should be subjected to disciplinary action in accordance with the applicable
regulations.
Therefore, since I have decided to issue the writs, I am of the view that this matter should be
called in three months' time from today in order to consider the action taken by the 2nd and 3rd
Respondents and ascertain their progress.
Conclusion
Based on the reasons adumbrated above, I grant relief as prayed for in prayers (b), (c), and (d)
of the Petition, without costs.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
